guide.a.supported_payment_providers:
Stripe, Square, and SumUp. Choose one in Settings and enter your API credentials. You can switch between them at any time.

SumUp only works with a limited set of currencies (mostly European currencies plus GBP, USD, and BRL). If your site currency isn't supported, the Settings page will refuse the credentials and tell you to pick a different provider.
guide.q.recommended_payment_provider: Which payment provider do you recommend?
guide.a.recommended_payment_provider: Stripe. The setup is a fair bit easier — you just paste in your secret key and the webhook is created automatically. SumUp is similarly quick (an API key and merchant code, with the webhook handled for you), but it's limited to certain currencies. With Square you need to create a developer application, find your location ID, and manually configure the webhook yourself. All three work well once set up, but Stripe gets you going faster.
guide.q.paid_ticket_booking_flow: What happens when someone books a paid ticket?
guide.a.paid_ticket_booking_flow: They fill in the booking form, then are redirected to your payment provider's checkout page. Once their payment is confirmed, their place is recorded and they receive their ticket. Their place isnot held while they're paying — see Why don't we hold places during checkout? below for the reason.
guide.a.reservation_window: When someone starts paying for a ticket, their place is reserved for 5 minutes. If they don't complete payment within that time, the reservation is released and the place becomes available for others. This prevents places being held indefinitely by abandoned checkouts.
guide.q.listing_sells_out_while_paying: What if the listing sells out while someone is paying?
guide.a.listing_sells_out_while_paying: If someone completes payment but the listing has since sold out, they are automatically refunded. They'll see a message explaining the listing is full and that their payment has been returned. This is rare but possible — it's the trade-off described in the previous question.
guide.a.how_refunds_work: See the Refunds section below for full details on automatic refunds, admin-issued refunds, and bulk refunds.
guide.a.what_is_booking_fee:
The booking fee is an optional percentage-based charge added to ticket prices at checkout. For example, if you set a 2% booking fee on a {ticketPriceFormatted} ticket, the attendee pays {totalWithFeeFormatted} in total.

Configure it in Settings under Booking Fee (only visible when a payment provider is set up). Enter a percentage between 0 and 10. Set it to 0 or leave it blank to disable. The fee is calculated on the subtotal and added automatically during checkout.
guide.q.find_stripe_secret_key: How do I find my Stripe secret key?
guide.a.find_stripe_secret_key:
1. Log in to your Stripe Dashboard
  2. Click Developers in the navigation menu
  3. Select API keys from the sidebar
  4. Under Standard keys, find the Secret key row and click Reveal
  5. Copy the key — it starts with sk_live_ for live mode or sk_test_ for test mode
  6. Paste it into the Stripe Secret Key field on the Settings page

Tip: Use a sk_test_ key first to verify everything works before switching to your live key. Test mode lets you make bookings without real charges.
guide.q.stripe_webhook_setup: Do I need to set up a Stripe webhook myself?
guide.a.stripe_webhook_setup: No. When you save your Stripe secret key in Settings, the system automatically creates a webhook endpoint in your Stripe account and stores the signing secret. You can verify it's working by clicking the Test Connection button that appears after saving your key.
guide.q.create_square_application: How do I create a Square application?
guide.a.create_square_application:
Before you can accept payments with Square, you need to create an application in the Square Developer Dashboard. This gives you the API credentials the system needs.

  1. Go to the Square Developer Dashboard and sign in with your Square account
  2. Click the + button to create a new application
  3. Give it a name (e.g. your organisation or listing name) and click Save

Once created, you can find your access token and location ID from the application's pages (see below).
guide.q.find_square_access_token: How do I find my Square access token?
guide.a.find_square_access_token:
1. Log in to the Square Developer Dashboard
  2. Select your application
  3. Open the Credentials page
  4. Copy the Access token for the environment you want (Sandbox for testing, Production for real payments)
  5. Paste it into the Square Access Token field on the Settings page
guide.q.find_square_location_id: How do I find my Square location ID?
guide.a.find_square_location_id:
1. Log in to the Square Developer Dashboard and select your application
  2. Open the Locations page in the sidebar
  3. Copy the Location ID for the location you want to accept payments at

You can also find your location ID in the main Square Dashboard under Account & Settings → Business information → Locations.
guide.q.setup_square_webhook: How do I set up the Square webhook?
guide.a.setup_square_webhook:
Unlike Stripe, the Square webhook must be configured manually. After saving your Square access token and location ID:

  1. Go to the Square Developer Dashboard and select your application
  2. Navigate to Webhooks in the sidebar
  3. Click Add Subscription
  4. Set the Notification URL to the webhook URL shown on your Settings page
  5. Subscribe to the payment.updated event
  6. Save the subscription, then copy the Signature Key that Square provides
  7. Paste the signature key into the webhook field on your Settings page

The webhook is what tells the system when a payment has been completed, so bookings won't be confirmed until this is set up.
guide.q.stripe_test_vs_live_keys: What is the difference between Stripe test and live keys?
guide.a.stripe_test_vs_live_keys:
Stripe provides two completely separate environments, each with its own set of API keys:

  • Test mode (sk_test_ / pk_test_) — a sandbox environment for development and testing. No real money is moved. You can use Stripe's test card numbers to simulate successful and failed payments. Bookings created in test mode won't appear in your live Stripe dashboard.
  • Live mode (sk_live_ / pk_live_) — the production environment. Real cards are charged and real money is transferred to your Stripe account.

The system detects which mode you are in based on the key prefix and shows it on the Settings page. Only keys with a valid prefix (sk_test_ or sk_live_) are accepted.
guide.q.test_or_live_credentials: Should I use test or live credentials?
guide.a.test_or_live_credentials:
Start with test credentials to make sure everything is working before accepting real payments. All three providers offer separate test environments:

  • Stripe: Use a key starting with sk_test_. You can make test payments with Stripe's test card numbers. The Settings page will show a Test mode badge so you always know which environment is active.
  • Square: Use your Sandbox access token and location, and tick the Sandbox mode checkbox on the Settings page. You can make test payments with Square's sandbox test values. Untick Sandbox mode when switching to production.
  • SumUp: Use an API key starting with sk_test_. As with Stripe, the Settings page shows a Test mode badge so you know which environment is active. Swap to your sk_live_ key to go live.

When you're ready to go live, replace the test credentials with your production credentials in Settings. For Stripe, the system will only accept keys that start with a valid prefix (sk_test_ or sk_live_).
guide.a.automatic_refunds:
A place is only ever counted once payment completes — nothing is held during checkout (see Why don't we hold places during checkout? above). Because of that, a completed payment can occasionally find that the booking is no longer possible, and in those cases the payment is refunded automatically. This happens when, by the time the payment is confirmed:

  • the listing has sold out — another buyer took the last spot first, so the slower payer is refunded and shown a message explaining the listing is full;
  • the price has changed — an admin edited the listing price mid-checkout, so the amount charged no longer matches the current price;
  • the listing has been closed or deactivated while the buyer was paying.

In multi-listing bookings it's all-or-nothing: if any single listing fails (e.g. one of the combined listings is full or its price changed), the entire payment is refunded — not just the portion for the affected listing.
guide.q.refund_individual_attendee: How do I refund an individual attendee?
guide.a.refund_individual_attendee: Open the listing's attendee list, find the attendee, and click Refund. You'll see a confirmation page showing their name, email, quantity, and the amount paid. Type the attendee's name to confirm and submit. The refund is issued through your payment provider (Stripe, Square, or SumUp) and is always a full refund.
guide.q.refund_all_attendees: How do I refund all attendees for a listing?
guide.a.refund_all_attendees: On the listing page, click Refund All in the navigation bar. Type the listing name to confirm. Each attendee with a recorded payment is refunded one by one. If some refunds fail (e.g. a payment was already refunded via the provider dashboard), you'll see a summary of how many succeeded and how many failed.
guide.a.partial_refunds: No. The system always issues a full refund for the total amount paid. If you need to issue a partial refund, do it directly through your payment provider's dashboard (Stripe, Square, or SumUp).
guide.q.attendee_after_refund: What happens to the attendee after a refund?
guide.a.attendee_after_refund:
The attendee remains registered. A refund only clears their payment record — it does not remove them from the listing. If you also want to remove them, delete the attendee separately after refunding.

Refunds are per-listing. If the attendee is registered for multiple listings, refunding one listing does not affect their other registrations.
guide.q.refund_free_listing: Can I refund an attendee who booked a free listing?
guide.a.refund_free_listing: No. The Refund button only appears for attendees who have a recorded payment. Free-listing attendees have no payment to refund.
guide.a.refund_fails: The most common reason is that the payment was already refunded directly through Stripe, Square, or SumUp. You'll see an error message like "Refund failed. The payment may have already been refunded." If your payment provider is no longer configured, refunds will also fail because there's no provider to process them through.
guide.q.refund_same_attendee_twice: Can I refund the same attendee twice?
guide.a.refund_same_attendee_twice: No. After a successful refund the attendee's payment record is cleared, so the Refund button no longer appears. If you attempt to refund a payment that was already refunded via the provider dashboard, the provider will reject it and you'll see a failure message.
guide.a.what_is_the_money_ledger:
Money shows every money change on your site. Each row says what happened and when.

Checkout and refund records cannot be changed or deleted. Later corrections stay beside the original records. This keeps the full history clear.

Simple view explains each change. Detailed view shows where the money moved. Select a linked name to see its running total. Each attendee has their own Money too.
guide.q.ledger_accounts_explained: What do the names in Detailed view mean?
guide.a.ledger_accounts_explained:
Most names are a listing, attendee, or option. You can select linked names to see their Money.

Three names have a fixed meaning:

  • Card / bank — money received from or returned to a customer.
  • Booking fees — booking fee income added to ticket prices.
  • Corrections — changes that keep the other totals correct.
guide.q.ledger_entry_kinds: What do the different money changes mean?
guide.a.ledger_entry_kinds:
Each change has a short label:

  • Booking made — ticket income recorded when someone books.
  • Payment received — a deposit or full payment was received.
  • Booking fee — booking fee income was added.
  • Price change — a discount or extra charge changed the price.
  • Refund — money was returned. The related booking, fee, and price changes were also removed from the totals.
  • Service event cost — a service event cost was recorded for a listing.
  • Correction — an earlier total was corrected.
  • Change reversed — an admin action exactly cancelled an earlier change.
guide.q.ledger_manual_entries: How do I record a waived amount or another money change?
guide.a.ledger_manual_entries:
Open Money for an attendee, listing, or option. Select Add money change. Choose what happened and enter the amount.

The new change updates the running total without changing earlier records. This option appears only where you can add a money change.
guide.a.how_daily_listings_work: Daily listings let attendees choose a specific date when booking. You set which days of the week are available (e.g. Monday to Friday), the minimum number of days before a date can be booked, and the maximum number of days into the future to show. The capacity limit applies independently to each date.
guide.a.what_are_bookable_days: These are the days of the week your daily listing runs on. If you only tick Monday and Wednesday, those are the only days that appear in the date picker. Weekends and unticked days are skipped.
guide.a.what_are_holidays: Holidays are date ranges when no daily listings can be booked. Add them from the Holidays page. Any dates falling within a holiday range are removed from the booking calendar for all daily listings.
guide.q.why_don_t_we_hold_places_during: Why don't we hold places during checkout?
guide.a.why_don_t_we_hold_places_during:
When someone clicks “Buy”, we don't reserve their place while they're paying. A place only counts as taken once the payment goes through. This might sound backwards, so here's why.

Imagine if we did hold places during checkout. A sneaky person could write a small program that opens the checkout page over and over, grabbing every place, without ever paying. Real visitors would see “sold out” even though nobody had actually bought anything. When the holds expired, the program could grab them all again. This is how ticket scalpers cause problems on bigger sites.

Because places only count once payment is finished, the only way to “hold” a place is to actually pay for it. Real money has to change hands — so the trick above doesn't work, and real visitors get a fair chance at the tickets.

The trade-off: very rarely, two people can finish paying for the last place at almost the same moment. The first payment to arrive wins; the second person is automatically refunded. See the next question.
guide.q.is_the_booking_fee_refunded_too: Is the booking fee refunded too?
guide.a.is_the_booking_fee_refunded_too: Yes. Refunds reverse the full charge taken from the attendee, including any booking fee that was added at checkout. Your payment provider's own processing fee is a separate matter — Stripe and Square each have their own policy on whether processing fees are returned on a refund, so check your provider for details.
guide.q.how_do_i_set_up_sumup: How do I set up SumUp?
guide.a.how_do_i_set_up_sumup:
SumUp uses its Hosted Checkout, and the webhook is handled automatically — there's nothing to configure in the SumUp dashboard. You need two values, and both must come from the same SumUp account:

  1. API Key — a secret API key from your SumUp dashboard. The developer settings are easy to miss: go to Profile → Settings → For Developers → Toolkit → API Keys, or use this direct link: me.sumup.com/en-gb/settings/api-keys. That page shows a Public API key near the top — that is not the one you need. Instead, in the API Keys section below it, click Create API key, give it a name, and copy the new (private) key — it is shown only once.
  2. Merchant Code — your SumUp merchant code (a short identifier, usually starting with M), shown in your SumUp dashboard under your profile/account settings.

Paste both into the SumUp section on the Settings page and save, then click Test Connection to verify they work. The test looks up your merchant account using the API key, so if the two don't belong to the same account — for example a sandbox API key paired with your live merchant code — it reports a 401 Unauthorized error. If you see that, re-copy the key in full and double-check the merchant code is the one shown in the same SumUp account that created the key.

SumUp only supports certain currencies. If your site currency isn't one of them, saving the credentials is blocked with a message asking you to choose a different provider.
